questions.q: Why was kdb+ specifically built the way it is, according to this lesson?
options: To replace spreadsheets for small business accounting

To ingest and query enormous volumes of continuously arriving tick-level market data, both live and historical, with extremely low latency, by keeping huge amounts of data in memory with a column-oriented engine
To provide a graphical interface for writing Python scripts
To serve as a general-purpose web application database
questions.explain: kdb+ exists because tick-by-tick market data is enormous and continuous, and general-purpose databases aren't built for keeping that volume in memory and answering queries against it with the extremely low latency that trading infrastructure needs.

questions.q: In the q reference snippet `` select avg price by sym from trades where sym=`AAPL`MSFT ``, what does `` `AAPL`MSFT `` represent?
options: A single string containing a typo
A symbol list -- kdb+'s categorical/enum-like type, written with backticks and no separators between items
A file path to a trades table
A comment that q ignores
questions.explain: q uses backtick-prefixed symbols as its categorical/enum type, and a symbol list like `AAPL`MSFT is written by concatenating multiple backtick-prefixed symbols with no separator -- it is not a string or a typo.

questions.q: How does q's vector-first philosophy differ from the vectorization mindset taught in Lesson 1 of this course (pandas/NumPy)?
options: q does not support vector operations at all

In q, operating on whole columns is the only idiomatic default and loops are the rare exception, whereas in Python/pandas vectorization is a discipline layered on top of a language that also permits loops freely
q requires explicit loops for every calculation, unlike pandas
Vectorization in q only works on integer data types
questions.explain: The lesson draws this exact contrast: Lesson 1 taught vectorized thinking as a habit to adopt within a language (Python) that also allows loops freely, while q was designed so vector/array operations are the only comfortable default from the ground up, with explicit loops reserved for genuinely unavoidable cases.

questions.q: According to the lesson, what actually justifies a quant team reaching for kdb+ instead of DuckDB/Parquet?
options: Having any dataset stored as a table
Wanting to avoid writing SQL
A genuine requirement for continuous high-frequency ingestion and live, low-latency queries against streaming data -- not simply because the data is time-series
Needing to store more than a few thousand rows
questions.explain: The lesson is explicit that DuckDB/Parquet already handle the vast majority of research workloads well; kdb+ earns its cost and learning curve specifically for tick-level, continuously streaming, low-latency production infrastructure, not for time-series data in general.

questions.q: How can a reader who wants to actually run q code themselves get access to kdb+, given that no installation was used in this lesson?
options: It cannot be run outside of a licensed trading firm
KX offers a free personal/non-commercial edition of kdb+ that individuals can install on their own machine to learn the platform and run q
q code can only run inside a Jupyter notebook with a special plugin
kdb+ is open source and bundled with every Python installation
questions.explain: The lesson notes that kdb+ is proprietary, but KX provides a free personal/non-commercial edition specifically so individuals can learn and run q themselves -- that installation, not this course's environment, is how the reference snippets here could actually be executed.
